messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eighteen months ago, Tane’s younger brother died after a night of reckless drinking, the final moments of his life defined by the sharp tang of spilled bourbon and a hospital staff member who had ignored his deteriorating condition. Tane had come to believe that his own life had been fundamentally shattered by that night, a conviction that settled over him long before any clinical assessment. He could not tell a clear story of what happened even to himself; the recollection of the emergency call arrived as a series of disjointed snapshots rather than a timeline. When he forced himself to remember, a heavy guilt would wash over him, followed by a chilling numbness where he felt completely detached, as if watching a stranger’s tragedy unfold. The environment around him quickly dictated his internal landscape. Whenever the scent of fermentation drifted from a passing colleague’s lunch or a patient’s jacket, the smell of alcohol instantly hijacked his recollection, dragging the fractured, guilt-laden images back into his conscious mind. At the pharmacy where he worked, a manager’s sharp reprimand for a misplaced schedule triggered his intolerance for moral violations, and the sight of people misbehaving without consequence would immediately pull him back to the night he realized no one had protected his brother. Even the sight of a passing funeral procession would force the cemetery grounds and grief-related imagery back into focus, making the past impossible to put down. The triggers did not just remind him of the event; they actively reconstructed the memory each time, pulling the fragments back to the surface. Those recurring, guilt-charged memories then dictated his environmental scanning. Because he could not process the trauma as a resolved story, his mind remained fixed on searching for the original dangers that had caused the loss. He found himself constantly checking grocery aisles for liquor sections and avoiding community gatherings where graves or mourning rituals might be discussed. The emotional residue of his guilt on recall acted as a compass, steering him away from any setting that might contain the alcohol smell or the casual disregard for safety he associated with the hospital staff. The memory of the event did not fade; instead, it constantly generated new triggers, ensuring that his attention never settled in the present. His conviction that his life had been destroyed and that nothing felt meaningful anymore did more than color his thoughts; it fundamentally wired his nervous system to expect catastrophe. Tane had come to believe that the world was inherently unsafe because he had lost the joy he used to feel, and this profound sense of meaninglessness kept his body in a state of perpetual readiness. His physical tension became constant, his shoulders locked and his breath shallow, as though he were perpetually bracing for another collapse. The negative appraisal of a ruined future directly amplified his physiological threat response, turning every minor disruption into a signal of impending doom. Conversely, the relentless physiological alarms solidified his pessimistic worldview. Tane often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, his heart racing and muscles coiling at a dropped syringe or a loud pharmacy pager. These false alarms convinced him that his body was breaking down, reinforcing his conviction that he had lost the capacity for happiness and that his life was irreparably damaged. The constant state of bodily alertness felt like evidence that he could never return to his former self, transforming a physiological reflex into proof of a shattered existence. Each panic spike validated the narrative of total loss. Over time, the belief that his life was destroyed deepened both his fragmented recall and his environmental hypersensitivity. Viewing himself as a person whose happiness was gone made the guilt on recall feel inescapable and the emotionless recall feel like a permanent state, stripping any attempt at processing of its hope. Simultaneously, the conviction that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore made him hyper-vigilant to moral violations and grief-related settings, as if the world were filled with the same careless forces that had taken his brother. Tane had come to seek help because the tightening loop finally made his work untenable; he could no longer function behind the counter when his body reacted before his mind could catch up. He was most afraid of remaining trapped in the numb, hyper-alert state, hoping instead to finally piece together a story that might allow him to live again.
